2025 EMEA Private Capital Outlook: Midyear Update
Introduction
In December 2024, we provided six predictions in our 2025 EMEA Private Capital 
Outlook. As we approach the midway point of 2025, we are checking in to see how 
our outlooks are trending. Private markets have experienced a complex landscape 
marked by liquidity challenges, strategic shifts, and emerging opportunities. Our 
outlooks cover key themes that we believe will shape activity in 2025.
A tougher dealmaking environment for portfolio companies has lingered in 2025. 
Interest rates are now flattening and coming down, as the latest rate cycle led to 
an increasing cost of debt for transactions. This has helped debt providers but 
has hurt those seeking debt to finance. As a result, strategies such as private debt 
and venture debt have gained attention. On the flipside, large deals that require 
substantial amounts of debt tied to elevated interest rates have fallen out of favour.     
The ongoing liquidity crunch has been top of mind for market participants. The 
lack of exits, particularly on the VC side, has provided a challenge for GPs to 
generate returns for LPs. Companies that were eyeing an IPO in 2025 are likely 
reconsidering given the fallout from announced US tariffs. Despite PE exits 
showing greater resilience, fewer distributions flowing back to LPs have given 
rise to secondaries transactions. Secondaries have emerged as a prevalent topic 
as investors seek liquidity solutions amid a volatile exit market characterised by 
uncertainty around valuations. 
The fundraising landscape has been mixed. PE GPs have closed major middle-
market funds and megafunds in recent quarters, pushing towards new records. 
Within VC, fundraising has been trending downwards since 2022, largely focused 
on large fund closes from established names. Fewer VC exits are resulting in less 
capital being recycled into new funding efforts.
Opportunities in sectors and regions persist despite the gloomy outlook. AI is 
everywhere, and the broadening range of applications is expected to promote 
activity. Geopolitical tension rages on, and this could create opportunities in lesser-
known regional pockets. If unpredictability persists in the US, investors may look 
elsewhere to allocate capital. However, a precarious global financial ecosystem 
remains as we move through 2025.

Rationale from December 2024
Middle-market fundraising includes fund sizes between €100 million and €5 billion. 
These often represent the heartbeat of the PE industry and exclude megafunds, 
which heavily skew fundraising data. In our series of analyst notes on The Rise 
of European Megafunds Part I and Part II, we explain how megafunds have been 
raising the bulk of the capital in recent years in Europe. As such, we prefer to look at 
middle-market fundraising to get a more accurate picture of the health of PE. Since 
peaking in 2021 at more than €70 billion in capital raised, middle-market fundraising 
in Europe has stalled and failed to surpass its 2021 levels. This was a result of two 
factors: deteriorating financing due to higher-for-longer interest rates and a muted 
exit market in which LPs have not been receiving distributions they can reinvest 
into fundraising. However, we expect 2025 to look much different from the previous

2025 EMEA Private Capital Outlook: Midyear Update
three years, reversing the middle-market fundraising trend back into YoY growth 
territory and finally surpassing its previous high. Deal activity in Europe recovered 
in 2024 and grew more than 35% YoY in value. If we extrapolate this growth for 
middle-market fundraising, we could expect a record year in capital raised across 
middle-market funds. Monetary easing and favourable economic conditions will be 
the driving factors behind this recovery in the short term. As for long-term secular 
trends, we expect PE as an asset class to continue growing its AUM as various new 
types of investors start allocating to PE.
Midyear update: Outlook is tracking better than expected.
Middle-market fundraising is off to a flying start YTD, accounting for two-thirds 
of the total capital raised in 2024 in just five months. At the current run rate, 2025 
middle-market fundraising could be expected to close €100 billion in new capital, 
which would be a record year and a 55.9% YoY increase. As expected, the recovery 
in PE dealmaking seen in late 2024 is beginning to translate into stronger fundraising 
activity in 2025. Q1 saw notable follow-on funds from CVC Capital Partners, Oakley 
Capital, Ardian, ICG, and Adelis Equity. Furthermore, Thoma Bravo, the US software 
buyout specialist, closed its first European-dedicated fund, securing €1.8 billion 
in Q1. This increased commitment from US PE firms to the European market has 
served as a key catalyst in accelerating European PE fundraising. Given the direction 
of travel of interest rates and the resilience seen in dealmaking YTD, we remain 
confident that middle-market fundraising in Europe in 2025 will surpass last year’s 
levels. That said, potential US tariffs could pose a risk if they lead to a market 
downturn, prompting LPs to scale back commitments due to the denominator effect 
from declining public market valuations, as discussed in our note, The Impact of 
Tariffs on European PE.

2025 EMEA Private Capital Outlook: Midyear Update
Outlook: PE GP-led secondary exits will grow by 
double digits.
Rationale from December 2024
In the latest cycle of monetary tightening from 2022 to 2024, a correction in market 
valuations led to a sharper slowdown in exits relative to deals. PE-backed public 
listings became scarce, sponsor-to-sponsor acquisitions were more expensive to 
execute due to higher borrowing costs, and corporates were squeezed for cash 
from the lower valuations and higher financing costs. This led PE sponsors to 
look elsewhere for exit liquidity, and secondaries emerged as the solution. Better 
guidelines around structuring GP-led secondary exits to align interests for all parties 
have also played a significant role, notably with the Institutional Limited Partners 
Association guidance published in April 2019. GP-led secondary exit value has more 
than doubled over the past five years, whilst exit counts have risen by even more, 
from 16 transactions in 2020 to 112 in 2024. In our analyst note, GP-Led Secondaries, 
we forecast that GP-led secondaries will grow globally at 13.2% per annum in our 
bull case. This would translate to a GP-led secondary exit value of at least $66 billion 
for 2025, and we forecast at least 100 transactions for the year.
Midyear update: Outlook is tracking with some variations.
2024 seemed to be a pivotal year for GP-led secondaries, which increased in 
popularity and offered liquidity to LPs and GPs alike. This type of transaction went 
from being relatively opaque for most sponsors to a viable exit solution, allowing 
sponsors to crystallise on their gains. 2024 finished as a record year for GP-led exits, 
reaching the upper end of our prediction of $50 billion to $60 billion. We have since 
seen new names dip into GP-leds, such as Ardian and Inflexion. Ardian launched its 
first-ever continuation vehicle to roll out its investment in Syclef. Inflexion raised 
the largest multi-asset continuation fund in Europe to date, closing on $3.05 billion 
across four assets in May. However, looking at our data YTD and accounting for our 
growth rate of 13.2% per annum, GP-led exit value is lagging in 2025. There are two 
potential explanations for this. First, it may be market-driven. The year has been

Rationale from December 2024
Venture debt has been a growing asset class and prevalent theme in European 
venture this year. A record €26.6 billion of deal value occurred in the continent in 
2024, as companies opted for cheaper financing, which has recently increased 
in availability. Whilst the cost of debt is cheaper than equity, other benefits have 
contributed to its increased usage, such as nondilutive financing, potentially faster 
access to capital, and extending cash runways through other means in between 
equity rounds. As discussed in our analyst note European Unicorns—Modelling 
Myth or Magic? this also enables a company to raise cash without having to 
rebase its valuations to current conditions, allowing for valuations to recover 
between rounds.
Venture debt has, therefore, proved popular amongst venture-growth players, 
with nearly two-thirds of deal value raised by such companies. These firms have 
had the scale and cash generation to take on debt but also require significant 
amounts of capital to grow further, which may prove more challenging if financed 
through equity. Deal value in 2024 was buoyed by six megadeals (value of more 
than €1 billion), which composed half of 2024 deal value. The most prolific user of 
venture debt, Northvolt, also demonstrated the risks associated with the strategy, 
with the company amassing more than €4.5 billion of debt before declaring 
bankruptcy in November. 
Therefore, whilst we think venture debt will remain an important and growing theme 
in the European venture ecosystem, we do not think deal value in 2025 will surpass 
2024. The absence of larger players such as Northvolt is a factor. However, more

broadly, companies that raised financing in 2024 are unlikely to come back to the 
cap table in 2025 when the term loan for such instruments occurs over several 
years. Firms could refinance debt amidst the lower-rate environment expected 
next year, but we believe new issuance is unlikely to eclipse the levels seen in 2024. 
Any YoY growth in 2025 would imply that deal value levels could reach 2021/2022 
heights, which we see as more of an anomaly than a trend. Furthermore, as we 
expect IPO markets to open next year, venture-growth players may opt to return 
to equity markets rather than debt. We suspect several companies would have 
undergone IPO due diligence over the last 12 to 24 months but did not pull the 
trigger because of unfavourable market conditions.
Midyear update: Outlook is tracking as expected.
As of 31 May 2025, venture debt deal value and volume are in line with our 
expectations for a more muted year of activity in 2025. YoY, the current run rates of 
activity so far imply a 31.5% and 49.9% decline in value and volume, respectively, 
with increasing deal sizes supporting value metrics. In absolute terms, €7.6 billion 
was raised in the asset class over 128 deals. Average deal sizes, therefore, increased, 
with the top three deals sitting close to or above €1 billion. These all sat in Sweden, 
the highest being €1.4 billion refinanced by United Petfood, €1 billion raised by car 
rental subscription service FINN, and €898 million raised by UK financial technology 
company Capital on Tap. By stage, venture growth still comprises the lion’s share, 
at two-thirds of deal value, with the late stage also increasing share, to 18% of value 
from 6% in 2024.
By lender, the top three names by number of all-time deals stayed the same. There 
was some movement elsewhere, with BNP Paribas adding 20 deals to its 10-year 
count and Barclays moving up from tenth to seventh place, with 10 historical deals 
added. There were some new names in the top 10 as well, such as US VC firm 
Western Technology Investment, with a heavy skew towards venture debt funds, 
which closed nine deals in Europe over the past year. Looking at the top lenders’ 
deal activity so far in 2025, volumes are sparse compared to 2024. However, outside 
of a supply perspective, demand for debt may be supported by more uncertainty 
in equity markets and a muted environment for IPOs (as discussed below). 
Nevertheless, it remains likely that activity in 2025 will not surpass last year’s levels.

Rationale from December 2024
In early 2024 we outlined our outlook for the European IPO market. Since then, our 
thesis has somewhat played out, with the VC-backed listing space producing more 
of a vent than a window through 2024 but with activity warming in the second half 
of the year. IPO exit value amounted to €11.2 billion in 2024. We have also previously 
noted that Puig’s IPO composed most of this value, as the Spanish luxury brand’s 
exit size was €10.9 billion. It is evident, therefore, that the broader market is not 
recovering as headline exit activity would suggest because only a few smaller 
listings have emerged. However, the factors we outlined as “handles” to open a 
window appear to have largely aligned through the second half of 2024 to provide 
a more favourable backdrop for listings in the new year. These include interest 
rates, valuations and share price performance, geopolitics, company-specific 
fundamentals, and profitability. 
Whilst the recovery in Europe has been concentrated, it is still important not to 
dismiss activity from larger transactions. Such may skew the data but are important 
for venture asset class returns and providing liquidity for LPs levered into European 
investments. Looking into 2025, we expected the recovery would continue to be 
concentrated. Klarna was the most obvious example, where the company filed for 
an IPO in the US. Whilst Klarna would not list on a European exchange, large listings 
need to occur to give confidence to venture stakeholders that the industry’s liquidity 
and returns are improving. It is also important to note that a rising tide would lift all 
boats and instil confidence in other European market participants to list. Whether 
or not that translates to activity on European exchanges remains to be seen, but 
ultimately, we believe market conditions and a healthy pipeline are favourable for 
2025’s IPO exit value to supersede 2024’s.
Navina Rajan
Senior Analyst, EMEA Private Capital
navina.rajan@pitchbook.com

10
2025 EMEA Private Capital Outlook: Midyear Update
Midyear update: Outlook is not tracking with some variations.
Unforeseen volatility from geopolitics has dominated financial markets and listings 
since the start of the year. Our thesis for an IPO window, published earlier this year, 
was predicated on five “handles” aligning towards the end of last year. One of those 
was geopolitics, where significant political events in Europe and the US (namely 
elections) had somewhat run their course and volatility and valuations had aligned 
to a sweet spot for listings activity to pick up. Whilst we acknowledge geopolitics to 
be a crucial pillar to our thesis, it was not possible to foresee the extent of impact 
Trump’s “liberation day” would have, the level and tone of tariffs the US government 
set out to implement, or the volatile nature of policy. We are, therefore, less 
optimistic about an IPO window in 2025. We believe this year is likely to look like 
2024, during which a few names came to market, but listings struggled to generate 
meaningful value and volume. 
Despite a less optimistic view, however, there are some puts and takes to IPO 
activity in Europe so far in 2025. €3.6 billion of listings have been generated over just 
four exits, leading to a concentrated level of activity. YoY, this could also be deemed 
somewhat of a recovery, as despite €11.2 billion of value last year, nearly all of that 
(€10.9 billion) was generated from the listing of Puig. Stripping Puig out, therefore, 
implies a significant uptick in activity YoY, although overall it should still be noted 
that numbers are small. 
The recent events in financial markets also do not bode well for the rest of the 
year in Europe, but several firms in the US have powered through uncertainty and 
chosen to IPO (including Coreweave, Hinge Health, and the Circle Group) despite 
valuations in Europe showing more resilience than in the US. Israeli firm eToro, 
which is included in our European data, also listed in the US in May. This is also a 
consideration moving forward, if more nationalistic policy and negative sentiment 
continues around the US market, whether financial stakeholders continue to adopt 
a more domestic approach. Overall, whilst our expectations appear to be partially 
playing out during the first half of this year, we continue to be cautious as to whether 
this will be the case by the end of 2025. Key listings such as Klarna, which could 
potentially list by the end of 2025, may swing activity to be more in line with our 
outlook. Previous candidates, such as SHEIN, have withdrawn from the UK after not 
receiving approval from Chinese regulators. Visibility remains low, and there are 
many factors that could sway activity either way in 2025. We believe risks to our 
outlook are still skewed to the downside.

Rationale from December 2024
AI has been talked about extensively across regions, sectors, and asset classes in 
2024. Tech giants are investing in the space, established companies are leveraging 
AI to drive efficiency, and new startups are increasingly aligning themselves to AI 
in creative ways. Multiple use cases have been highlighted across everyday life for 
businesses and consumers. It has been challenging to avoid the frenzied attention 
AI has garnered, so we expect investment to be strong in 2025 and anticipate 
new PE and VC deal activity records will be set in Europe. Not only are companies 
competing, but also countries and continents are vying to become AI powerhouses 
and drive innovation for future generations. European governments and bodies 
have recognised the role large US tech companies have had in powering growth 
for several years via stock market returns, investment into local ecosystems, 
and job creation. Therefore, we expect a renewed focus on Europe developing its 
own tech behemoths. 
The speed of development is another consideration for new records to be set in the 
AI space. US-based OpenAI raised €5.9 billion in 2024 and is valued at a staggering 
€141.3 billion, roughly five times its €26.4 billion valuation in 2023.1 There is no doubt 
AI companies are hot at the moment, but it is the rapid progress they are showing 
that is driving up figures. Another example is France-based Mistral AI, which was 
founded in 2023 and became a unicorn a year later and now possesses a €6 billion 
valuation after a €600 million round in 2024. We expect more of these stories to 
emerge in 2025 as capital deployment in the AI industry intensifies.

2025 EMEA Private Capital Outlook: Midyear Update
Midyear update: Outlook is tracking as expected. 
€7.6 billion and €4.2 billion were invested in VC and PE AI deals, respectively, in 
the first five months of the year. The current run rate puts new records in sight, 
but further dealmaking at a similar pace throughout the year will be required. One 
transaction lifting the total in 2025 YTD was the €1.4 billion buyout of UK-based 
AI content creation business Metaphysic. Another notable deal involved Google 
DeepMind’s drug discovery spin-off, Isomorphic Labs, which raised €536 million. 
Contrasting industries such as video content and drug discovery highlight how AI is 
impacting multiple use cases and attracting capital. 
Europe’s AI industry is experiencing significant growth, driven by strategic 
investments and technological advancements. Areas such as infrastructure linked 
to energy consumption of power-thirsty data centres and the advancement in 
semiconductor development provide further opportunities. Policy and regulation 
changes are evolving too, including the EU’s Artificial Intelligence Act. Overall, the 
current AI boom is being labelled as a revolutionary leap akin to the introduction of 
the internet or the smartphone era.

Rationale from December 2024
The growing influence of capital sources originating from the Middle East and 
North Africa (MENA) region has been touted for several years, and we believe 
this will continue in 2025. As of 30 November 2024, private market fundraising 
reached $14.6 billion, and we anticipate this figure will grow in 2025. Capital raised 
by MENA-based funds exceeded $20 billion for the first time in 2022 and grew to 
$37.1 billion in 2023. Whilst fundraising dipped in 2024, we expect a rebound above 
$20 billion in 2025. The growth will be largely driven by the development of fund 
managers targeting different asset classes, local regional tech ecosystems, and the 
progression of capital market usage in the region. Moreover, we feel favourable tax 
and pro-business policies will entice more individuals, corporations, and investors to 
commit capital to the area. 
Diversification of revenue streams, leveraging government support, and developing 
partnerships with experienced investors are priorities for nations in the Middle East. 
As a result, funds are cropping up in a range of sectors, including real assets, green 
energy, tourism, and IT. Fundraising activity will be reinforced by a combination 
of domestic and international LPs, as well as substantial government resources. 
Numerous initiatives, such as the ambitious Saudi Vision 2030, are resulting in 
copious amounts of investment across sectors. Various projects are underway in 
healthcare, infrastructure, logistics, entertainment, real estate, and finance. We 
expect these elaborate plans will keep capital flows elevated and investment parties 
interested in raising funds in the region.
Midyear update: Outlook is not tracking as expected. 
Only $2.1 billion has been raised across 17 funds in the MENA region YTD. Therefore, 
a significant uptick in fundraising will be required to reach our $20 billion outlook
